The Rosario Islands excursion takes you from Cartagena to the archipelago's clear Caribbean waters, beaches and coral reefs. Over five hours, you will cross Cartagena Bay by speedboat, see Bocachica and its old forts, and then have free time by the sea on the archipelago's main island.

Hotel pickup is scheduled for 9:00. After the transfer to Bodeguita Pier, the speedboat journey begins. The crossing to the islands takes approximately 45 minutes, with views of Cartagena Bay, Bocachica and the San Fernando and San José fortresses along the way.

The boat passes Barú Island and then arrives at the main island of the Rosario archipelago. You will have free time to enjoy the waterfront and use the island's facilities.

The original programme also specifically highlights the coral reefs, colourful fish and sea turtles that are part of the archipelago's natural environment.

From the airport on Baltra Island, you will travel to the Itabaca Channel, which separates Baltra from Santa Cruz. The crossing by motorboat takes approximately 5 minutes, after which the journey continues by private vehicle across the island towards Puerto Ayora.

The natural scenery changes along the way, from the drier northern areas to the island's green highlands. As you travel through Santa Cruz's agricultural areas and wild landscapes, you may see giant land tortoises.

The programme also visits giant tortoise habitats and the famous lava tunnels. You can walk for around 30 minutes through preserved sections of the lava tubes and see how they were formed.

## North Seymour Island and Bachas Beaches

This excursion day offers a remarkable opportunity to visit North Seymour Island and Bachas Beaches. We will travel by bus to our yacht in the Itabaca Channel, then sail for an hour to North Seymour. We will land on a rocky shore beside a small forest of grey and silver Palo Santo trees, which remain leafless for much of the year.

North Seymour is a true jewel of the Galápagos Islands, where the variety and untamed beauty of nature are extraordinary. Volcanic landscapes dotted with silvery-grey Palo Santo trees create an unforgettable sense of peace and harmony. Every step brings a feeling of adventure as you watch magnificent frigatebirds swaying in the wind and blue-footed boobies performing their famous dances.

## Quilotoa Lake Is a Volcanic Lake in the Western Andes!

You will reach Quilotoa, a volcanic lake in the western Andes at an altitude of 3,900 metres. One of Ecuador's most beautiful and spectacular destinations, it stands out for its peaceful natural surroundings and its green and turquoise waters within an ancient volcanic crater. You can walk down to the shore to admire the water up close. It is an ideal place to relax and enjoy the tranquillity of nature. The climb back up is good exercise but requires effort. Alternatively, local residents rent mules to travellers who need help reaching the rim. After visiting the lake, you will have lunch at a restaurant run by the indigenous community living in the area. The drive to Quilotoa follows scenic roads, and travellers will also visit Pujilí, Zumbahua and Tigua, picturesque traditional Andean communities that continue to preserve their customs and culture. On Saturdays, the Zumbahua indigenous market takes place, offering vibrant colours and a lively glimpse of this important tradition. Tigua is particularly known for its community of visual artists, whose colourful paintings depict indigenous Andean life and landscapes.

## Quilotoa Lake — an Extraordinary Natural Wonder of Ecuador!

## Quilotoa Lake — a Wonder Hidden in an Ancient Volcanic Crater, Its Waters Shimmering in Turquoise and Emerald!

Quilotoa is a volcanic lake in the western Andes, at an altitude of 3,900 metres. It formed in the crater of an extinct volcano and is known for its picturesque turquoise and green waters. The lake attracts visitors with its impressive scenery and the tranquillity of the surrounding nature. Here you can hike, descend to the shore and enjoy the lake's beauty up close. The Quilotoa area is also renowned for the traditions and culture of its indigenous peoples.

The city is known for its squares, fountains and colonial buildings associated with the era of cotton plantations.

Many facades are covered in tiles imported from Portugal, Germany and France. This decoration has become one of the most distinctive features of the old town.
